how-much-to-charge.html.text:
← Water heater replacement bid calculator

How much should I charge to replace a water heater?

Homeowners search "how much to replace a water heater" and get back one number. A same-day 50-gallon electric tank swap in a garage is not a condensing tankless install on a 3/4-inch gas upsize with a sidewall vent and an attic carry — and a flat installed price cannot see which job it's quoting. Price the heater type, the location, the vent, and the gas or electrical path instead.

Open the free water heater bid calculator

What a flat installed price cannot see

Tank vs. tankless vs. heat pump. Each has its own equipment cost, install hours, and venting requirement. A straight tank swap and a tankless conversion are different jobs, not different price tiers of the same job.

Access. An attic or crawl-space carry adds real labor a closet or garage swap never sees.

Venting. B-vent and concentric sidewall venting are different materials and different labor, and a tankless conversion frequently needs a vent change the old tank never had.

Gas and electrical upsizes. A tankless unit's higher BTU input can require a 3/4-inch gas line upsize; some units need dedicated 240 V circuits and panel work. Neither shows up in a "swap the tank" price.

A bid you can defend

  1. Price the heater type — tank, tankless, or heat pump — and its own equipment and labor.
  2. Add access hours for attic or crawl-space work.
  3. Price the actual vent path, not the old one.
  4. Add a gas-line upsize or electrical/panel work where the new unit needs it.
  5. Load the wage, then add overhead, and price = cost ÷ (1 − target margin) for a walk-away number.

The calculator does that arithmetic in your browser. Capacity hints are starting points, not a first-hour rating, fuel-gas table, or manufacturer clearance you can stamp or submit — confirm sizing and code compliance with a licensed plumber or electrician.

Worked example

A same-day 50-gallon electric tank swap in a garage, no venting to change and no access penalty, is a straightforward, comparatively quick job. A condensing tankless conversion in the same house, on a 3/4-inch gas-line upsize, a new sidewall vent, and an attic carry to reach the old unit, is several times the labor and material — before either quote has priced dollars per gallon of capacity delivered. The calculator prices both from the same inputs so "how much to replace a water heater" never has to guess which swap it's quoting.

Common questions

How much should I charge to replace a water heater?

There is no flat installed price. A same-day 50-gallon electric tank in a garage is a different job from a condensing tankless on a 3/4-inch gas upsize with a sidewall vent and an attic carry. This calculator prices the heater type, the location, the vent, and the gas or electrical path from your own wage and material inputs.

Is this a plumbing-code ruling or a first-hour-rating calculation?

No. Outputs are arithmetic on the numbers you enter. Capacity hints are starting points, not a first-hour rating, fuel-gas table, or manufacturer clearance you can stamp or submit.

    How much does upsizing the gas line add to a tankless bid?

    On a 10-foot run at this calculator's default wage, burden, overhead, and margin, moving a gas tankless from "existing line looks adequate" to a 3/4-inch upsize adds 4 labor hours and $270 in materials — about $804 more on the bid ($1,525.94 to $2,329.59). Most 1/2-inch lines that fed the old atmospheric tank cannot flow enough gas for a condensing tankless, so pricing the existing line as reusable is how a competitive-looking bid loses money on the first callback.

    At this calculator's defaults, a 7 GPM electric tankless priced on "existing circuit looks adequate" comes to $1,433.20. The same job priced on the panel work an electric tankless usually needs — two or three dedicated 40 A 240 V circuits, not the single 30 A breaker the old tank used — comes to $2,700.97: 3.2 more labor hours and $620 more in electrical materials, about $1,267.77 higher. Pricing the old circuit as reusable on an electric tankless is the electrical-side version of the gas-line mistake above.

vs-a-flat-rate-water-heater-special.html.text:
← Water Heater Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat-rate water heater special

"$1,200 water heater installed" is not a price for a job — it is a price for a same-day tank swap in an easy garage, quietly reused for every house that also asks to replace a water heater.

What a flat water heater special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote over the phone: read off the postcard or search-result number, skip the walkthrough. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of job — usually a 50-gallon electric tank swapped in a garage or basement with easy access, the existing circuit reused, no vent change, no gas work — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one needs an attic carry, a condensing tankless, a gas-line upsize, or a panel rebuild.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the heater type (electric tank, atmospheric or power-vent gas tank, condensing gas tankless, electric tankless, or heat pump), tank gallons or tankless GPM, location, venting and vent length, gas line and gas-line length, electrical path, and add-ons such as an expansion tank, drip pan, condensate, recirculation pump, haul-away, seismic straps, a mixing valve, and tankless service valves, plus your own loaded wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin. It returns the installed price, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money — for this heater and this house, not a flat number for every garage.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a same-day 50-gallon electric garage swap or a condensing tankless on an attic carry with a gas-line upsize — several times the labor and materials for the same phrase "water heater". Prices the heater from the entered type, capacity, location, vent, and gas or electrical path, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Has no line for upsizing a 1/2-inch gas line to 3/4 inch, regardless of whether the existing line can actually flow enough gas for a condensing tankless. Prices the gas line separately by scope and length, and flags when a tankless is being priced on an existing line that "looks adequate" — the check the flat rate never runs.
Quotes the same number for a heater set on the floor and one carried into an attic or crawl space, with no separate line for access hours. Times attic, crawl, closet, and basement access as their own labor hours, on top of the base swap.
Has no line for a concentric sidewall vent, a drip pan, a condensate line, or tankless service valves — the extras a condensing or heat-pump unit usually needs that the old atmospheric tank did not. Prices venting by type and length and each add-on as its own labor and material line, applied only when the job calls for it.
Gives the installer a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper flyer. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against what a flat special would have quoted the same job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two houses, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own shipped defaults — a $48 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, 16% overhead, and a 25% target margin:

The easy job — a 50-gallon electric tank swapped in a garage, existing circuit reused, no vent change, no gas work, with an expansion tank and haul-away — prices at $1,035.40, on a job that costs $776.55 to run.

Take the same house to a condensing gas tankless in the attic instead — a concentric sidewall vent, a 3/4-inch gas-line upsize, a drip pan, a condensate line, tankless service valves, and haul-away — and the job costs $2,984.49 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator bids it at $3,979.33: 3.8 times the easy job, on the same "water heater replacement" phrase. Quoting the attic tankless at the easy job's own $1,035.40 flat rate prices it $1,949.09 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $2,943.93 it falls short of this calculator's own bid price at the same 25% target margin. Same flat rate, one house that pays and one that loses money the moment the attic carry and the gas upsize show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat water heater special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and materials scale with heater type, location, vent, and gas or electrical path, not with the word "water heater" alone. A same-day 50-gallon electric tank swapped in an easy garage is a different job from a condensing gas tankless carried into an attic on a 3/4-inch gas upsize with a concentric sidewall vent, a drip pan, and a condensate line. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

The vent, the gas or electrical path, and the attic or crawl-space access hours. A rate built around "swap the tank" has no line for upsizing a 1/2-inch gas line to 3/4 inch, no line for a concentric or PVC sidewall termination a condensing unit needs instead of the old atmospheric stack, and no line for the extra hours an attic carry takes over a garage that is already at floor level.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped defaults, at a $48 hourly wage, 30% payroll burden, 16% overhead, and a 25% target margin: the easy job -- a 50-gallon electric tank in a garage, existing circuit, no vent, no gas work -- prices at $1,035.40, on a $776.55 break-even cost. Move the same house to a condensing gas tankless in the attic instead -- concentric sidewall vent, a 3/4-inch gas upsize, a drip pan, a condensate line, and tankless service valves -- and the job costs $2,984.49 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator bids it at $3,979.33: 3.8 times the easy job. Quoting the attic tankless at the easy job's own $1,035.40 flat rate prices it $1,949.09 below its own break-even cost.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote a water heater swap?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs -- same heater type, easy garage or basement access, no vent change, no gas or electrical work -- a flat rate can land close, because that is probably the job the rate was set on. The risk is applying it outside that band without noticing, because the postcard rate does not know which band a given house is in and neither does the installer until the walkthrough.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local labor rates, equipment cost, or what competitors charge. It takes the heater type, location, vent, gas or electrical path, and add-ons, plus your own loaded wage, burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a walk-away price for the job you describe -- the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat water heater special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

This calculator vs. ServiceTitan

Two different shapes: ServiceTitan is an account-based field service management platform for running a plumbing company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one water-heater replacement cost, given its type, location, vent, and gas or electrical path, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceTitan is a field service management platform, founded in 2007 by Ara Mahdessian and Vahe Kuzoyan, headquartered in Glendale, California. It is used by plumbing, HVAC, electrical, and other trades for scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, marketing, reporting, and job costing across a whole business, with a mobile app for crews in the field. It is an account-based platform: you sign up and use it as an ongoing service across a whole company, not a one-off calculator. ServiceTitan's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — field service management software serving the plumbing trade among others, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceTitan appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceTitan does. It does not schedule technicians, dispatch crews, or invoice a customer, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one water-heater replacement's heater type (electric tank, atmospheric or power-vent gas tank, condensing gas tankless, electric tankless, or heat pump), tank gallons or tankless GPM, location, venting and vent length, gas line and gas-line length, electrical path, and add-ons — expansion tank, drip pan, condensate, recirculation pump, haul-away, seismic straps, a mixing valve, and tankless service valves — plus loaded installer wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the installed price, the price per gallon or per GPM, the effective hourly rate, and a comparison against a typical 50-gallon electric garage swap at the same rates — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears the walk-away floor, and a single printable customer proposal for that one job. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
